notes:
I found plenty from the older commentators (Calvin, Gill, Ellicott, Clarke, Barnes, Poole, Pulpit, Spurgeon) and from Guzik, Constable and Ironside. The coverage has some gaps:

- **Denominational differences:** None of the pages I read showed one Protestant tradition disagreeing with another on these verses. What I did find were disagreements between individual commentators, and I've marked those as "Differences." I've added each writer's tradition (Calvin and Poole Reformed, Gill and Spurgeon Baptist, Clarke Methodist) from my own background knowledge. The pages themselves don't say it.
- **Thin verses:** I found little or nothing specific on vv. 70–75 and v. 77.
- **Not found:** NET Bible notes, an Orthodox commentary (I only found a Protestant site describing Orthodox worship), and any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. Those are left out.

**v. 54–55**
- Barnes: the promise mainly in view is the Messiah, now about to arrive. But it also covers the other mercies God gave Israel. He links "forever" back to "in remembrance of His mercy," meaning God's mercy is to be remembered forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-56.htm
- Barnes also says these verses close Mary's song by praising His special goodness to his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-56.htm

**v. 56**
- Did Mary stay for John's birth? Calvin (Reformed) and Poole (Puritan) think she probably did. Calvin says she stayed to see God's grace at work and to have her faith confirmed. Poole thinks she left soon afterwards. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_56-66.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-56.htm
- **Differences:** Bengel says she left before the birth. Ellicott thinks it likely she waited, but notes that v. 57 seems to suggest she had already gone. Coffman calls the question unanswerable from Scripture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-56.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-56.html
- Gill (Baptist): three months was the period Jewish teachers set for confirming a pregnancy. When she got back to Nazareth, Joseph noticed she was pregnant (Matthew 1:18). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-56.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist): even with such a future ahead of her, Mary would not neglect the duties of her home. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke

**v. 57**
- Guzik: The promise was fulfilled just as God said it would be. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Luk/Luk_1.cfm

**v. 58**
- Calvin: we can't tell whether the neighbours praised God just for the birth or had already heard about the angel's promise. Either way, a child born to a barren woman of great age was no ordinary favour. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_56-66.htm

**v. 59**
- Clarke (Methodist): Jewish boys were named at circumcision, and the first-born usually got the father's name. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-59.html
- Constable: Jews usually named children at birth and Greek-speaking Jews a few days later. That custom may explain why John was named at his circumcision. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-59.html
- Calvin: circumcision drew a crowd because it was a shared sacrament of God's people, not meant to be done privately. He adds that believers should choose names that teach their children, such as the names of godly forebears. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_56-66.htm

**v. 60**
- Guzik: both parents knew the angel had commanded the name John (1:13). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Calvin isn't sure Elizabeth spoke by inspiration. He thinks Zechariah probably told her the angel's instruction in writing. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_56-66.htm
- Several sources explain that John means "the LORD is gracious." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-13.html

**v. 61–62**
- **Differences: was Zechariah deaf as well as mute?** Guzik says the relatives treated Zacharias as if he were deaf, not mute. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Constable disagrees: Zechariah apparently couldn't hear either, and the Greek word used for his condition can mean deaf as well as dumb. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-63.html
- Ellicott agrees with Constable. Everyone's surprise in v. 63 only makes sense if Zechariah hadn't heard the argument. https://biblehub.com/luke/1-63.htm

**v. 63**
- Ellicott: tablets were wood covered with wax. The present tense "is" is emphatic, because the name had already been given. Gill makes the same point. https://biblehub.com/luke/1-63.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-63.html
- Sproul (Reformed): Zechariah showed whether custom or God's word governed him. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/birth-john-baptist
- Guzik: this was faith stating a fact, and God gave Zechariah a second chance at faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Luk/Luk_1.cfm

**v. 64**
- Ironside: Unbelief had closed his lips; faith opened them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/isn/luke-1.html
- Calvin: God held back the cure until this day so that people would look at John. By praising God, Zechariah also admitted publicly why he had been punished. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_56-66.htm

**v. 65–66**
- Calvin: the fear was awe at God's power. God uses miracles to wake up dull minds, not to entertain. He also notes that few remembered these wonders once John began preaching. He reads "the hand of the Lord" as a figure of speech for God's power plainly at work. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_56-66.htm

**v. 67–68**
- Guzik: the prophecy proves it is truly from the Spirit because it speaks first of the unborn Jesus, not of John. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Utley: Zechariah thanks God for sending the Messiah. John doesn't come in until vv. 76–77. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-1
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the song Jewish in form, but Christian in sentiment. It splits it into two parts: thanks for Israel's hopes fulfilled (vv. 68–75) and words to John (vv. 76–79). https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02473a.htm
- **Liturgy:** Catholics say it every morning at Lauds (morning prayer) and at burials. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/benedictus
- **Lutheran:** It is used in Matins and Morning Prayer. https://witness.lcms.org/2021/christmas-canticles/
- **Orthodox (described by a Protestant site):** It is among the biblical "Odes" sung at matins. https://www.gotquestions.org/Book-of-Odes.html
- **Modern scholarship:** Most scholars doubt Zechariah composed the song on the spot. Some suggest early Jewish Christians wrote it, or Luke himself. https://voice.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-benedictus/
- Loisy guessed it was an older psalm that Zechariah adapted. The Catholic Encyclopedia says there are "grave objections" to that view. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/benedictus

**v. 69**
- A horn stands for power, so "horn of salvation" means a mighty deliverance from David's house. It restores Israel's hope, but in a higher, spiritual sense. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/benedictus
- Guzik: Jesus is the horn of salvation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 70–75**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the deliverance fulfils the oath to Abraham. But its purpose is not worldly power: it is so that God's people can serve Him without fear, in holiness. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/benedictus
- Bible Hub's topical article says this section stresses God's faithfulness to the Abrahamic covenant. https://biblehub.com/topical/z/zechariah's_prophecy--the_benedictus.htm

**v. 76**
- "Go before the Lord" points to Isaiah 40:3. John later applied that verse to himself, and all three Synoptic Gospels use it. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/benedictus

**v. 77**
- Guzik: John would teach the knowledge of salvation and point people to forgiveness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Lutheran (1517): John's ministry of repentance and forgiveness still prepares people today to receive Christ. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-song-of-zechariah

**v. 78**
- Ellicott: "tender mercy" is literally "bowels of mercy," the Jewish way of speaking of God's heart. "Dawn" means sunrise. In the Greek Old Testament the same word also stood for the Messianic "Branch" (Jeremiah 23:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-1.html
- Gill, Poole and Maclaren take the Dawn to be Christ. Maclaren connects it with Malachi's "Sun of Righteousness." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-78.htm
- **Protestant vs Catholic:** Poole adds that forgiveness depends on God's free love, not upon our satisfactions and penances, (as papists dream). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-78.htm
- **Interpretive difference:** JFB says the Dawn is either Christ or the light He gives, and that either way the sense is the same. Philpot (a Strict Baptist, from my own knowledge) says the dayspring is not the sun itself but the first light announcing it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/luke-1.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jcp/luke-1.html
- **Text note:** Some manuscripts read "hath visited" and others "shall visit." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-78.htm

**v. 79**
- **Difference: who gives the light?** Guzik says John would give light and guide people into peace. Gill says these words belong to the Dawn (Christ), not to John the Prophet of the Highest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-78.html
- Spurgeon applies the verse to personal comfort and to missions. The gospel goes to those in darkness, and it comes before civilisation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-78.html

**v. 80**
- Guzik: the desert is where God trains many of His prophets. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- **Where in the wilderness?** Barnes puts it in the hill country near Hebron. Gill suggests Ziph or Maon, not the place John later preached. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-80.html
- **Modern debate: was John an Essene?** Constable thinks probably not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-80.html
- Desiring God allows John may have known the Essenes, but shows how he differed: he preached to all Israel. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/was-qumran-the-cradle-of-christianity
- Bible.org lists the similarities but concludes John was no Essene. https://bible.org/seriespage/witness-dead-sea-scrolls
- GotQuestions says it is possible but can't be proven. https://www.gotquestions.org/Essenes.html
- **Catholic:** John lived in the wilderness to discipline the body and seek holiness. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-pain-of-stolen-honey
